docs.text: Ouroboros or-uh-bore-us Extract ROIs from cloud-hosted medical scans. Ouroboros is a desktop app (built with Electron) and a Python package (with a CLI). The desktop app uses Docker to build and run its Python server. For this reason, Docker is required to run Ouroboros. If you are interested in using the Python package for its CLI or for a custom usecase, check out the python folder in the main repository. Ouroboros also has a Plugin System . Plugin servers are also run in Docker. Usage Guide It is recommended that you read these pages in order. Download and Install Ouroboros Slicing Backprojection Plugins Reference Technical Constants - hardcoded file explorer limits and plugin broadcast behavior. Large Folder Behavior The Ouroboros File Explorer is designed to open scan and output folders directly, but it is not a general-purpose file browser. It loads subfolders on demand: opening a folder shows only that folder's direct entries, and subfolder contents stream in when you expand each subfolder. When you point it at a folder that contains many files or deeply nested subfolders, the following behavior applies: Only the root's direct entries are loaded up front. Nested subfolders are loaded and watched only when you expand them. Collapsing a subfolder keeps its state and watcher alive for a short window (thirty seconds by default) so quickly re-expanding is free. If you leave it collapsed past that window, the underlying watcher is torn down and the subfolder's cached children are dropped from renderer state; re-expanding later behaves like a fresh load. The panel stops loading new paths after one hundred thousand visible entries across all currently open watchers. When this happens, Ouroboros shows a warning toast asking you to pick a smaller folder or expand the folder in smaller pieces. node_modules , __pycache__ , venv , and any directory whose name starts with . are always skipped. See Technical Constants for the exact values, why they were chosen, and when to adjust them. Ouroboros Explanation A user of Ouroboros may have a multi-terabyte volumetric scan, hosted with the Neuroglancer family of tools (i.e. cloud-volume ). Perhaps there is a long, relatively sparse structure (ROI), like a nerve or a blood vessel that crosses the entire scan. Even with a well-equipped computer, it would be difficult to segment the entire stucture in one pass due to RAM limitations. Ouroboros provides a solution. A user first traces the structure in Neuroglancer with sequential annotation points, and then saves the JSON configuration to a file. Ouroboros opens this configuration file and cuts rectangular slices along the annotation path, producing a straightened volume with the ROI at the center of each slice (usually much smaller than the original scan). Every tenth slice in a circular annotation path, rendered in Ouroboros's Slicing Page. From there, the user segments the much smaller straightened volume with their choice of segmentation system. Then, Ouroboros backprojects the segmented slices into the original volume space (unstraightens it), producing a full segmentation.

docs.text: Development Docker and WSL troubleshooting Start with the README's Development Quick Start . It owns the installation, launch, and interactive verification sequence. This page covers backend verification and conditional troubleshooting; run commands from the repository root unless stated otherwise. Verify and rebuild the development backend Close the installed Ouroboros app and other development instances before launching. Development and installed apps share the ouroboros-server container name, ports, and ouroboros-volume volume. Do not use a running released container as evidence that the current branch is being tested. npm run dev starts both the Docker backend (port 8000) and the host volume-transfer service (port 3001). Starting Compose alone does not start that host service, which is needed to transfer inputs and deliver results. After launching, inspect the running container: docker inspect ouroboros-server --format '{{json .Mounts}}' docker logs --tail 50 ouroboros-server In the mounts, the source for destination /app/ouroboros must correspond to this checkout's python/ouroboros directory (Docker Desktop may translate the host path). The logs should show Uvicorn watching /app/ouroboros and completing application startup. If the mount is absent or points to another checkout, stop the app that owns that server and restart development from the intended checkout. python/compose.dev.yml uses the normal Python Dockerfile for dependencies, binds the checked-out package at /app/ouroboros , and enables Uvicorn reload. Source edits in that package do not require an image rebuild. After dependency or Dockerfile changes, close the development app, rebuild, then relaunch using the README sequence: docker compose -f python/compose.dev.yml build ouroboros-server Docker Desktop is running but WSL cannot connect A missing socket error such as this means the development shell cannot reach Docker: failed to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock connect: no such file or directory In Docker Desktop, enable the WSL 2 engine and Settings → Resources → WSL Integration for the specific distribution running development, then apply the changes. If integration settings are absent, check that Docker Desktop is using Linux containers. Retry docker info in the same WSL shell you use for npm run dev ; it must return server information. Docker Desktop being open, or a container running elsewhere, does not verify this connection. See Docker's WSL integration instructions . Electron uninstall after npm ci Electron's binary must be installed before electron-vite reads Electron's path.txt . An otherwise successful dependency installation can end with Error: Electron uninstall at launch if that file is missing. Run the explicit install-electron step in the README. It uses Electron's bundled installer ; no custom downloader is needed. Check the installed executable with: npm exec --no -- electron --version This verifies executable installation, not the GUI or Docker connection. JSON paths and folder selection Paths must be valid for the operating system running Electron. Linux Electron inside WSL needs /mnt/c/... or /mnt/wsl/... , not C:\... or \\wsl$\Ubuntu\... . Native Windows Electron uses Windows paths. Use File → Open Folder , choose the containing folder, then drag the JSON from the app's file explorer into Neuroglancer JSON . The slicing page currently ignores JSON changes before a working folder has been selected, even when the typed absolute path is valid. In the GTK folder picker, Ctrl+L lets you enter an absolute folder path. Conditional X11 file-picker workaround A forwarded X11 session can leave the desktop portal without a usable display. Check the portal logs for Failed to open X11 display and failure to associate the dialog with its parent. A nonfunctional window's title alone does not establish the cause. For this portal/X11 mismatch, close the development app and launch with: GDK_BACKEND=x11 npm run dev -- -- --xdg-portal-required-version=999 Both -- separators are intentional: npm consumes the first, and electron-vite forwards the arguments after the second to Electron. The portal-version switch selects the native GTK dialog when the portal does not meet that version requirement; GDK_BACKEND=x11 uses the app's X11 display. This workaround applies to a portal/X11 mismatch; verify the file picker and WebGL preview separately. WebGL preview failures The slicing page's React Three Fiber Canvas in VisualizeSlicing.tsx draws the 3D slice/bounding-box preview. These repeated messages indicate that its WebGL context could not be created: THREE.WebGLRenderer: A WebGL context could not be created. GL_VENDOR = Disabled, GL_RENDERER = Disabled, Sandboxed = yes ErrorMessage = BindToCurrentSequence failed The app does not explicitly disable hardware acceleration and currently provides no preview fallback for context creation failure. A functioning file picker and successful backend processing are separate from a functioning preview. Capture the failing launch Record the launch command, Electron version, and DISPLAY , WAYLAND_DISPLAY , and XDG_SESSION_TYPE from its shell. Distinguish a WSLg session from forwarded X11. Check Microsoft's WSL GUI/OpenGL prerequisites for WSLg. Capture the preview error from the renderer's DevTools console ( F12 in development) and GPU messages from the launch terminal. For Chromium logging and a main-process debugger, add --inspect before electron-vite's -- and --enable-logging after it: npm run dev -- --inspect -- --enable-logging . Retain any display settings and other Electron switches from the failing launch. Attach a Node debugger to the inspector address printed in the terminal (electron-vite 5 defaults to port 5858). In that main-process debugger, collect Electron's app.getGPUFeatureStatus() after GPU initialization ( gpu-info-update ), and app.getGPUInfo('complete') , including any rejection. These APIs belong to app from electron , not the renderer's console. Use diagnostics from the actual failing app; an isolated probe alone does not establish its GPU state. Software-rendering launch For the affected environment, close the development app and retain the working file-picker configuration while selecting the bundled SwiftShader driver: GDK_BACKEND=x11 npm run dev -- -- \ --xdg-portal-required-version=999 \ --use-gl=angle \ --use-angle=swiftshader These Chromium driver switches render on the CPU and may be slower than hardware acceleration. They apply to this launch and require no source changes. Do not use --disable-gpu or --no-sandbox as the standard fix. Verify the preview in the development app and retain any graphics warnings in the diagnostic report. Do not add --enable-unsafe-swiftshader merely to suppress a fallback warning. Other build paths Installed apps use the server image pinned by digest in the release lock . Docker pulls a missing image; the installed app does not build a server wheel or image. Local plugin installation explicitly builds Compose after copying the plugin into the app data folder, when its new backend files become available. The plugin template uses plugins/plugin-template/backend/compose.dev.yml during npm run dev-backend , mounts backend/app , and runs FastAPI development mode. Rebuild that Compose service after dependency or Dockerfile changes; ordinary source edits use reload. The packaged backend/compose.yml stays unchanged. Keep GPU-specific containers in plugins or optional Compose overrides. The core server does not require CUDA; segmentation plugins such as SAM-backed plugins are the appropriate place for CUDA runtime bases.

docs.text: Production package flavors The release workflow builds the flavors selected by release/release-lock.json for each supported desktop runner. The available flavors are: core : Ouroboros only, with the production server compose file pointing at the registry-published server image. with-plugins-cpu : the core package plus bundled Neuroglancer and Automatic Segmentation plugin artifacts. The automatic segmentation plugin uses its CPU backend image. with-plugins-cuda : the core package plus bundled Neuroglancer and Automatic Segmentation plugin artifacts. The automatic segmentation plugin uses its CUDA backend image and Docker Compose GPU reservation. Plugin flavors stage bundled assets in separate resource directories inside the external packaging workspace. Electron Builder maps each flavor's resources into the installed extra-resources directory, including extra-resources/preinstalled-plugins . The app installs those bundled plugin folders into the user plugin directory on startup. Release inputs The release lock is the only source of production pins and selected flavors. Update it to change the server image or bundled plugins; there are no separate per-image or per-plugin workflow inputs. The application version must match the lock's releaseVersion . The server is pinned by registry repository, immutable image digest, and source commit. Plugin inputs are pinned by repository, release tag, asset filename, SHA-256, and source commit, with separate CPU and CUDA backend identities. Packaging verifies downloaded archive hashes and requires plugin-release.json to match the locked release identity. Backend image verification follows the corresponding lock entry. See the lock for current versions and digests. The packaged extra-resources/package-flavor.json records the selected flavor, release-lock hash, server image metadata, and exact plugin identities, including the verified plugin release metadata. This file describes the package; the release lock remains authoritative. If plugin release repositories are private, set OUROBOROS_RELEASE_ASSET_TOKEN to a token that can read those release assets. The workflow falls back to GITHUB_TOKEN when that secret is not set. Build and publication Pull requests run release preflight checks without building native installers. Native builds run on main , compiling Electron once per operating system and packaging each selected flavor. On CI, build workspaces, generated resources, dependency trees, plugin downloads, and final artifacts live under RUNNER_TEMP , outside GITHUB_WORKSPACE ; the source checkout is read-only input. Electron Builder uses an explicit application-file allowlist rather than packaging the checkout. Source files and installed dependencies are copied once into an external tree where Electron is compiled. Every flavor packages that same compiled application and dependency tree, with npmRebuild: false enforced. Flavor preparation and cleanup affect only that flavor's resources and output directory. The shared compiled tree remains available across flavors and is removed at the end of the run; there are no links back to checkout dependencies. A successful main build records the exact source commit, input lock, artifact sizes, and SHA-256 hashes. The tag-triggered publication workflow verifies those prebuilt artifacts and creates a draft release without rebuilding Electron or the server. See the release pipeline guide . Dependency auditing uses npm run audit:release against locked dependencies. Any reviewed audit exceptions are defined in the audit validator . Local checks Run the fast release preflight from the repository root: npm run preflight:release It validates the lock, application version, and packaging configuration, and exercises disposable external staging without compiling Electron, downloading plugin assets, or producing installers. Build all locked flavors on the corresponding native platform: npm run build:release-artifacts -- --platform linux Use mac on macOS or win on Windows. Scratch files and final artifacts default to RUNNER_TEMP , or the operating system's temporary directory when running locally without that variable. The command prints the final output location. Set OUROBOROS_RELEASE_ARTIFACT_DIR to choose another destination beneath that temporary root. It must be an absolute path outside the checkout and must be new or empty; existing artifacts are not cleared. Scratch files are removed after the run, while final artifacts are retained. The existing build:linux , build:mac , and build:win commands use the same staging and packaging entrypoint. For a local single-flavor build, select a flavor already present in the lock, for example: OUROBOROS_PACKAGE_FLAVOR=core npm run build:linux npm run build:unpack creates an unpacked application for the current platform through that entrypoint and prints its external location. Preparation and renaming scripts are internal build steps, not standalone checkout commands. Plugin downloads use the workspace's cache. To seed it with local release archives, set OUROBOROS_PLUGIN_ARTIFACT_DIR to an external directory that does not overlap the checkout or build inputs and outputs. Its contents are copied into the owned workspace cache; the original directory is never modified. Copied archives must match the filenames and SHA-256 values in the release lock. Stale copies are replaced within the workspace, without changing the originals or overriding the locked plugin identities.

docs.text: Registry Server Images The Python server image has a separate build lifecycle from desktop installers. Production packages use the image digest pinned in release/release-lock.json , so application startup pulls the image instead of building it locally. Published Image The Build and Certify Server Image workflow tests Python changes, builds the wheel, and builds python/Dockerfile-prod on pull requests. PR runs do not publish an image. On main , the workflow publishes sha-<full-commit> and records the registry repository, image digest, and source commit in a certified server manifest. A later release-lock update selects that image for desktop packages. Application version tags do not rebuild the wheel or server image. Base Image Pin Both Python Dockerfiles keep the readable thehale/python-poetry tag paired with an immutable digest. When upgrading that base, review the upstream image, resolve the new tag's digest, and update the tag and digest in python/Dockerfile and python/Dockerfile-prod together in the same reviewed change. Do not refresh the digest without an intentional base-image review. Release Compose Usage Release packaging derives extra-resources/server/compose.yml and extra-resources/server/server-image.json from the release lock inside its external workspace. These generated files are package outputs, not editable production image pins. The source checkout remains unchanged. The generated compose file preserves the production ports, ouroboros-volume mount, host.docker.internal mapping, OUR_ENV=docker , and shm_size settings, but uses image: instead of build: . Production first launch therefore pulls the published GHCR image instead of building the server locally. To change the packaged server, update the lock's serverImage entry using the certified server manifest. There are no per-image workflow inputs or preparation commands that override the lock. Use the package build entrypoint to stage and build desktop packages. Development compose files still build locally from source so local edits do not depend on registry state. Manual Runs The server workflow also supports workflow_dispatch for testing and publishing the selected revision. Desktop releases still consume its certified digest through the release lock; dispatching the server workflow does not change that lock or publish a desktop release.

docs.text: Shared-memory ownership python/ouroboros/helpers/mem.py owns shared NumPy allocation, attachment, serialization, and release. Its lifecycle handling adapts lftomo/util/mem.py at 8d4c884 : non-owning serialization, cleanup guards, and manager cleanup after owner death. Ouroboros does not import lftomo's role-based reuse planner or storage interfaces; there are no consumers of those facilities here. Allocation and handoff The manager server's shared_memory_context is the sole registry of managed allocations. Each entry contains a live SharedMemory handle and the allocation's release policy. list_segments derives its answer from that registry, which implements the standard library's shared-memory tracker interface. SharedNPArray() and TermedNPArray() allocate through the same server RPC. The server establishes ownership before returning a name. The client opens a local attachment and constructs array views; failed client attachment or view construction releases the server allocation. Inherited ShareableList() registration also opens an owning server handle before acknowledging the client. Serializing SharedNPArray transfers only its name, original shape, dtype, and view description. Deserialization opens a non-owning attachment; it does not transfer unlink authority or cached NumPy data. The server keeps the buffer alive even if the producer exits before the consumer opens it. This matters on Windows, where the allocation disappears when its last handle closes. Release and failure handling Run-scoped arrays and standard manager allocations live until manager shutdown. Termed arrays are released by remove_termed() at the existing per-volume completion point in VolumeCache.remove_volume() . They do not accumulate until shutdown. Validation and owner release are atomic at the server; an unknown or run-scoped name is rejected without closing the supplied array. On POSIX, release unlinks the name and closes the manager's handle. Already-open attachments remain valid until they close; new attachments cannot open the name. On Windows, release closes the manager's handle. Existing attachments keep the allocation alive until they close. The supplied array, when present, is closed after the server acknowledges release. Closing a deserialized attachment never unlinks the creator's allocation. Explicit array cleanup is idempotent and handles partial construction. Normal manager shutdown uses SharedMemoryServer.shutdown() and that same owning registry. A client-side shutdown() override would be replaced by BaseManager.start() 's finalizer and is not used for allocation cleanup. The manager detaches from the owner's POSIX process group, as in lftomo, so it can clean up after that group is killed. A watcher waits on Python's parent-process sentinel on all supported platforms; owner death releases tracked allocations and exits the manager. POSIX SIGTERM to the manager also triggers cleanup. Forcibly killing the manager itself cannot execute its cleanup code; Windows closes its handles, while POSIX retains its standard resource-tracker fallback. The server tracker and startup hooks depend on CPython manager internals. Native CI exercises Python 3.11 and 3.12 on Linux, Windows, and macOS. Tests prove producer exit before receiver attachment, per-buffer release, surviving mapped consumers, serialization authority, failed construction, normal/exception shutdown, and owner termination. Multiprocessing coverage includes the live server code. docs.text: Status presentation This document is the presentation reference for slicing, backprojection, and the autoseg plugin. It defines display semantics, not backend states or readiness rules. Each repository maps its existing observations at render time. Do not store the mapped values as another execution or connection authority. Display status Meaning Appearance Waiting A step is pending or an expected observation is awaited. Neutral Running The source reports that work is active. Blue Complete The source reports successful completion of this step. Green Warning A reported condition needs attention; it does not establish task failure. Amber Failed The source explicitly reports failure of the named operation. Red Interrupted The source explicitly reports interrupted execution. Red Unknown The available observation does not establish the state or outcome. Neutral Use Complete , not Succeeded or Completed, on state labels; use Failed , not Error, for an operation's state. Sentences can say “Slicing completed.” Notice severity ( info , success , warning , error ) describes a message, not execution state. Contextual labels such as Connected or Loads on first run are appropriate when they describe the actual observation more precisely than a generic state. Main-app step values pending/running/succeeded/failed/interrupted map to Waiting/Running/Complete/Failed/Interrupted . Autoseg's pending/in_progress/completed/error/warning normally map to Waiting/Running/Complete/Failed/Warning . These are display adapters; wire values stay unchanged. A known source-specific meaning takes precedence over blindly translating a string: autoseg's lazy ML-runtime warning means the model is not loaded yet, so it uses neutral Loads on first run , not a startup failure. The backend summary and checklist show separate observed facts. In the main app, launch-command completion does not establish backend readiness. A reachable backend plus a failed local launch displays Connected — local launch failed , with Failed on the launch row and Connected on the connection row. With no local launch observation, omit that row. Do not create additional probes to fill out a checklist. Autoseg's backend and browser volume observations must be named separately, since they can disagree. Task percentages describe their reported stages. They do not establish the overall outcome. Show the reported terminal result independently of notice dismissal. Communication trouble or a missing job does not establish Failed; preserve existing last-reported information and identify an unknown outcome where already observed. Keep workflow-specific stages rather than inventing a universal lifecycle. The main app's STATUS_LABELS and StatusLabel own its display vocabulary and state appearance. Plugin views follow this document through their local display adapter. A shared cross-repository runtime package is not required. Notices Use compact notices beside the information they explain: launch diagnostics in the initialization section; submission, task, and communication diagnostics in the task section. Keep the reported text and failure-stage details, including statistics-report messages. Long paths and messages wrap, and explicit line breaks remain readable. Severity uses a subdued background and border with these accents: info #a9ceff , success #a7ddb5 , warning #f3d18b , error #ffb3a8 . Errors announce with role="alert" ; other notices use role="status" . A request diagnostic has a visible, keyboard-accessible Dismiss button. Reported outcomes, steps, launch observations, and communication warnings remain source-derived and do not disappear when that diagnostic is dismissed. The main app moves only task-start request failures ( /slice/ , /backproject/ ) and previous-task deletion failures into these retained notices. Local form/input errors (including invalid options and Neuroglancer JSON), filesystem warnings, and rendering errors keep their existing global alerts. A moved failure is not also shown as a toast. ServerContext remains the owner of request errors; there is no copied notice history or page-local dismissal flag. Dismiss clears only that request's error, preserving results, pending state, and task/stream data. A new submission clears its earlier start and deletion notices before preparing the request. Successful requests retain their existing error-clearing behavior. Input editing or an unrelated successful request does not clear a retained diagnostic. Unlike autoseg's error list, these notices follow the existing request lifecycle rather than accumulating past failures. Undismissed errors retain the existing provider lifetime and can still be seen on returning to a page. A dismissed error cannot reappear on navigation because it was cleared at its owner. Persistence is limited to the provider's lifetime. Each deletion request is identified by its actual task-specific URL ( /delete/?task_id=… ), so one workflow cannot display another workflow's deletion failure. The saved task response remains the source of that task ID until the existing deletion/submission lifecycle replaces it.

docs.text: Benchmarking Runnable benchmark scripts live in python/benchmarks/ . Run the commands below from the repository's python/ directory with the project environment installed. Keep raw reports, logs, profiles, and specimen inputs in a work directory outside the source tree. Record important findings and validation evidence in the associated pull request or issue. Bounding-box partitioning The bounding-box reference describes the production estimator, partition selection, and external annotation manifest. Regenerate complete recorded paths and compare their geometry without fetching specimen voxels: Geometry reports use the production payload estimator, sVC + 8V + 12HW , which counts the native source, one float64 coefficient workspace, and one reused float32 coordinate plane. Direct TIFF writes contribute zero heap output bytes for every assignment. These estimates and chunk-coverage metrics are separate from measured slicing RAM and timing. .venv/bin/python benchmarks/benchmark_partitioning.py \ --fixtures /path/to/local-inputs --repeats 2 --output /tmp/partitioning.json The report includes allocation components, slice assignments and bounds, cumulative requested source bytes, chunk coverage, and partitioner elapsed time. Code-derived payloads and logical chunk bytes are separate from measured RAM, network traffic, and slicing throughput. Full-path runtime comparisons require the original source datasets and complete recorded options. Run-statistics overhead The real-data harness compares reporting disabled and enabled around the existing SliceParallelPipelineStep or BackprojectPipelineStep duration. This includes downloads, computation, output writes, cleanup, and worker/manager startup and shutdown inside that step. Earlier geometry/source setup, sampler startup/shutdown, and final report formatting and delivery are excluded. The separate Pipeline.process() timer covers the broader pipeline. Memory collection also covers that broader window, so collector CPU or sweep costs must not be divided by the shorter data-step duration and called overhead. See the run-statistics reference for metric definitions, platform differences, sampling coverage, and report boundaries. From python/ , with the project's virtual environment installed, reuse saved slice/backprojection options and choose a new work directory: .venv/bin/python benchmarks/benchmark_run_statistics.py \ --real-slice-options /path/to/slice-options.json \ --real-backproject-options /path/to/backproject-options.json \ --work-dir /tmp/ouroboros-real-data --workers 12 --pairs 2 --timeout 3600 This copies original annotations, preserves the image source/scientific settings, and visits every annotation path from shortest list to longest. Use --annotation-layer "Exact path name" to select a path without editing the annotations; repeat the option for multiple paths. Selection is recorded and checked when resuming. Both the data-operation and pipeline timing boundaries are recorded without adding production timers. Each pair runs slicing then backprojection of that exact output. Output headers, times, logs, options and reports remain; scientific TIFFs are removed after matching backprojection succeeds. No pixel hashing is performed. Failed trials remain recorded and dependent backprojections are marked skipped; remaining independent trials still run. A missing usable RAM sample is retained as a coverage failure, not silently treated as a disabled collector. An incomplete pair receives no aggregate overhead estimate. --resume-real-data completes an interrupted batch without repeating completed/failed attempts, after checking production code, annotations, settings and dependency versions. Retain all results; do not retry/select favorable trials or enlarge a workload merely to conceal costs. --workers must be a multiple of four. Sandbox execution must permit the existing multiprocessing manager sockets. Other harness modes These modes use broader timing windows than the data-operation comparison. Validate Docker report delivery separately from native timing diagnostics. # Existing local fixture; time Pipeline.process(), including preparation. .venv/bin/python benchmarks/benchmark_run_statistics.py \ --scope pipeline --reuse-fixture /tmp/ouroboros-local-fixture \ --work-dir /tmp/ouroboros-pipeline-overhead --pairs 3 # Generate a local fixture and time the full CLI handler. .venv/bin/python benchmarks/benchmark_run_statistics.py \ --work-dir /tmp/ouroboros-statistics-benchmark --pairs 7 The default deterministic fixture is a 384³ uint16 precomputed volume with 64³ raw chunks / 1 µm isotropic voxels. docs.text: Backprojection After straightened volume produced by the slicing step is segmented, Ouroboros's Backproject Page can be used to project the segmentation back into the coordinate space of the original volume. Using the Backproject Page Basic Usage Demo Reusing Options from a Previous Run See the same section under Slice Page . Compression Options One of the options on the Backproject page allows the user to configure the output compression format. Common options zlib zstd none (no compression, not recommended) For more information, see Tifffile , the Python package responsible for the compression. Output Position Offset By default, the slicing output tiff image is backprojected into the space of its minimum bounding box, rather than the space of the entire source scan. The offset of the minimum bounding box is stored in the output tiff's description metadata. It is also stored in the configuration file (which is modified by the backproject step). Plugin Segmentation Inputs The Straightened Volume File can be the segmentation TIFF produced by the autoseg plugin, as long as it was generated from the same slicing configuration selected in Slice Options File . Ouroboros checks the plugin output before backprojection: Shape must match the slicing config as D/V/U : number of slices, slice height, slice width. Single-stack TIFFs use page count for D ; directory outputs use the number of TIFF files. Dtype must be a mask-friendly integer or boolean type: bool , uint8 , or uint16 . Compressed plugin TIFFs are accepted when tifffile can read them; Ouroboros rewrites compressed or non-memmappable inputs to an uncompressed temporary stack before processing. Shape mismatches, dtype mismatches, and missing slice configuration report separate errors so plugin output problems do not require manual reshaping to diagnose. Slicing Options 📁 - Drag and drop files from File Explorer panel into this option. 📁 Straightened Volume File - Path to the volume of slices to backproject (e.g. the output tif of the slicing step). 📁 Slice Options File - Path to the -slice-options.json file which includes the information needed for backprojection. 📁 Output File Folder - The folder to save all the resulting files into. Output File Name - Base name for all output files. Output MIP Level - The MIP level to output the backprojection in (essentially an upsample option). Use this if you downsampled in the slicing step; downsampling changes are currently ignored. Upsample Order - The interpolation order Ouroboros uses to interpolate values from a lower MIP level. If you check the binary option, feel free to set this to 0. Backprojection Compression - The compression option to use for the backprojected tiff(s). Recommended options: none , zlib , zstd . Output Single File - Whether to output one tiff stack file or a folder of files. Performance Logging - Off by default. Enable to save detailed performance statistics beside the outputs. Progress bars and step timings remain available when off. The setting is saved with your options; older options files without it load with logging off. The saved preference applies to desktop runs; CLI runs require --verbose regardless of the saved preference. Output Min Bounding Box - Save only the minimum volume needed to contain the backprojected slices. The offset will be stored in the -configuration.json file under backprojection_offset . This value is the (x_min, y_min, z_min). Binary Backprojection - Whether or not to binarize all the values of the backprojection. Enable this to backproject a segmentation. Offset in Filename - Whether or not to include the (x_min, y_min, z_min) offset for min bounding box in the output file name. Only applies if Output Min Bounding Box is true. Process Count - Number of parallel processes to use during the backprojection process. Reducing the count trades parallel throughput for lower memory usage. Inspect memory use on the intended workload when choosing a count. Chunk Size - Size of each dimension (x/y/z) of the processing chunk. Increasing will increase memory usage; performance is a more complex tradeoff and making it too large will negatively affect performance. How Does Backprojection Work? A large amount of helpful data is saved in *-configuration.json file after the slicing process. This data contains all of the rectangle corners from slicing, and the bounding boxes the slices are associated with. With this data, Ouroboros recalculates the 2D coordinate grids of 3D points for each slice. Trilinear Interpolation Backprojection iterates through 3D chunks of the straightened volume, as follows following order: The chunks are loaded from a memory map of the straightened volume. A custom rapid trilinear interpolation implementation is used to map the slice data into a sparse representation of the backprojected volume, limited to a bounding box containing only points associated with the chunk. These sparse representations are written to disk intermediates, with individual files for each slice of the backprojected volume they are associated with. As chunks are completed, it evaluates which slices of the backprojected volume can be fully written by completed chunks. The data for these slices are loaded from the intermediates, then written to disk in the target folder as they are completed. Once all slices are completed, they are converted to a single file if this configuration option is enabled. Why Is Interpolation Needed? The slices in the straightened volume were originally produced through interpolation. Each slice has a 2D grid of 3D points, and the values at these points were approximated through interpolation. In order to put the data back, we have to interpolate in the opposite direction. Each point contributes to the value of its neighbors based on how close it is to them.

docs.text: Ouroboros Plugins Recommended Plugins Neuroglancer Plugin Embeds Neuroglancer as a page in the app. Supports loading from and saving to JSON configuration files in Ouroboros's File Explorer. Has additional features like fullscreen mode and screenshots. Assisted Automatic Segmentation Plugin Coming Soon! Based on Segment Anything, it attempts to automatically segment the ROI. Benefits from the assumption that the desired structure is centered in each slice. Supports human input via bounding boxes and positive or negative annotations. Installing a Plugin Open the Plugin Manager: File > Manage Plugins . Press the Plus Icon Paste the GitHub URL of the plugin. Press Download (Ouroboros downloads and installs the plugin for you) Where are plugins installed? In the appData /ouroboros folder. This folder is different on each OS. Preinstalled Production Plugins Production packages can bundle plugin folders under extra-resources/preinstalled-plugins/<plugin-name>/ . On startup, Ouroboros copies missing bundled plugins into the normal user-data plugin folder before it loads plugins. Bundled plugin installs are idempotent and version-aware. If a user already has the same plugin installed, Ouroboros compares the version field in each plugin's package.json ; it upgrades only when the bundled version is newer and skips existing installs that are current, newer, or not safely comparable. Creating a Plugin See the template README for more information. Directory Context in Plugin Iframes When Ouroboros posts a send-directory-contents message to plugin iframes, the payload contains the selected directory's directoryPath and directoryName but the nodes field is always an empty object. This broadcast fires on every root change and is intended as a notification only — plugins should not depend on receiving the full recursive file tree through it. To read the directory tree, plugins request it explicitly with the request-directory-contents message described below. Requesting Directory Contents Plugins ask the provider for the entries of a folder (optionally recursive) by posting a request-directory-contents message. The provider replies with a send-directory-contents-response message addressed only to the requesting iframe. Request (plugin → provider): window.parent.postMessage( { type: 'request-directory-contents', data: { path: '/absolute/path/under/current/root', recursive: true, // optional; defaults to false requestId: 'abc-123' // optional; the provider echoes it back } }, '*' ) Response (provider → requesting iframe): window.addEventListener('message', (event) => { if (event.data?.type !== 'send-directory-contents-response') return const { path, nodes, requestId, error } = event.data.data // `nodes` is a path-keyed nested map of { name, path, children? } // `error` is present only when the request could not be fully served: // - code: 'denied' path outside the current root, or no root open // - code: 'not-found' path does not exist / is not a directory // - code: 'limit' enumeration hit the aggregate cap; `truncated: true` // and `nodes` holds the partial result // - code: 'internal' unexpected error; see `message` }) If requestId is omitted from the request, the provider generates one and echoes it back on the response so plugins can still correlate. Path-traversal guard. Requests for paths outside the current root are rejected with code: 'denied' . Plugins get exactly what the user can see in the File Explorer and nothing above it. Truncation. When the aggregate visible-path budget ( FILE_EXPLORER_WATCH_LIMIT ) is exceeded mid-walk, the enumeration stops and the response is returned with error.code: 'limit' , error.truncated: true , and a partial nodes map. Callers issuing recursive requests on very large trees should be prepared to handle this. Ignore rules. The same ignore filter the File Explorer uses (dotfiles and the node_modules , __pycache__ , venv segments) applies here. Plugins cannot bypass it. For details and the values behind other file explorer limits, see the Technical Constants reference.

docs.text: Slicing Slicing is one of the primary features of Ouroboros, available in the CLI and the desktop app. Using the Slice Page Basic Usage Demo Reusing Options from a Previous Run Slicing Options 📁 - Drag and drop files from File Explorer panel into this option. 📁 Neuroglancer JSON - Path to the Neuroglancer configuration JSON file (exported from Neuroglancer with {} icon, or through the Neuroglancer Plugin) Neuroglancer Image Layer - Select Neuroglancer image layer to slice from. Neuroglancer Annotation Layer - Select Neuroglancer annotation layer to slice from. Slice Width - The output width of each slice image. Slice Height - The output height of each slice image. 📁 Output File Folder - The folder to save all the resulting files into. Output File Name - Base name for all output files. Annotation MIP Level - The annotation layer's MIP level. 0 is the highest resolution. Output MIP Level - The MIP level to output slices in (essentially a downsample option). 1 is a good starting point. Slicing Parameters Distance Between Slices - The distance between each slice along the annotation path. Use Adaptive Slicing - Rather than just using equidistant slices, add more slices in more curved areas. Adaptive Slicing Ratio - 1 indicates to consider distance and curvature equally, 0.5 is biased towards distance, and 2 is biased towards curvature. Output Single File - Whether to output one tiff stack file or a folder of files. Performance Logging - Off by default. Enable to save detailed performance statistics beside the outputs. Progress bars and step timings remain available when off. The setting is saved with your options; older options files without it load with logging off. The saved preference applies to desktop runs; CLI runs require --verbose regardless of the saved preference. Bounding Box Parameters Max Depth - Limits how many times a bounding box can be subdivided. Reaching this limit can leave a large task. Target Slices Per Box - Sets the slice-count target for the reference partition used to limit cumulative requested volume. The slicing partitioner seeks smaller task payloads within that allowance; this value is not a hard slice-count or RAM limit. Lowering it does not guarantee lower peak memory. See Bounding box partitioning . How Does Slicing Work? Spline Fitting Ouroboros fits a spline curve to the annotation path from the Neuroglancer JSON file. This produces a smooth, differentiable curve along the length of the annotations. If the line segments between annotation points were used, then there would could be highly discontinuous slice transitions around sharp corners. Slice Coordinate Frames Ouroboros calculates equidistant points along the spline curve. Each point is "1" apart from the previous to match the appearance of isotropic slices taken from one of the axes of the coordinate space of the full volume (the coordinate space of the annotation points). To follow any possible path, each point must have its own coordinate frame normal to the spline. For easier segmentation, it is also important that the axes of the point coordinate frames don't flip between points. To achieve this, Ouroboros calculates rotation-minimizing frames based on the change in orientation of the tangent vectors of adjacent points. Rectangles and Grids Ouroboros calculates the corners of the slice rectangle at using each point and its associated coordinate axes (as vectors). Pseudocode width_vector # 'u' unit vector scaled to slice width / 2 height_vector # 'v' unit vector scaled to slice height / 2 top_left = point - width_vector + height_vector top_right = point + width_vector + height_vector bottom_right = point + width_vector - height_vector bottom_left = point - width_vector - height_vector Then, for each point, a 2D grid is generated with given dimensions (slice width and height). Each point in the 2D grid is a 3D point which is calculated by interpolating between the four corner points. Volumes and Cubic Interpolation At this point, Ouroboros has a full grid of 3D points associated with each slice, but has yet to download any data from the cloud-hosted volume. Ouroboros groups slices into bounding boxes, using the full rectangle corners to keep every slice inside its assigned volume. It evaluates several spatial and path-order splits to reduce the largest estimated slicing-task payload. The selected partition requests no more cumulative volume than the reference partition made with the same bounding-box options. Geometry and subdivision limits can prevent further improvement; the partitioner does not measure available RAM or guarantee that a run will fit in memory. docs.text: Spline Fitting Ouroboros fits a spline curve to the annotation path from the Neuroglancer JSON file. This produces a smooth, differentiable curve along the length of the annotations. If the line segments between annotation points were used, then there would could be highly discontinuous slice transitions around sharp corners. Each point is "1" apart from the previous to match the appearance of isotropic slices taken from one of the axes of the coordinate space of the full volume (the coordinate space of the annotation points). To follow any possible path, each point must have its own coordinate frame normal to the spline. For easier segmentation, it is also important that the axes of the point coordinate frames don't flip between points. To achieve this, Ouroboros calculates rotation-minimizing frames based on the change in orientation of the tangent vectors of adjacent points. docs.title: How Does Slicing Work?

docs.text: Bounding box partitioning The slicing pipeline groups slice rectangles into source-volume requests. Its partitioner seeks to reduce the largest estimated slicing-task payload without increasing the cumulative requested source volume relative to the reference partition for the same options. It does not inspect available RAM, schedule workers by memory usage, or impose a hard task-memory limit. Geometry and assignment Every slice is assigned to exactly one box. A box's bounds enclose all four corners of every assigned rectangle; centers are used to propose splits, not to decide how much source data to retain. The requested integer extent runs from floor(min) through ceil(max) , inclusive on each axis. Downloads, slice grids, and backprojection use the same integer origin. Requested regions outside the source remain zero-filled. BoundingBox owns these integer extents. download_volume_geometry converts them to the half-open requests expected by CloudVolume and computes source clipping. The cost model uses the full allocated extent, including any zero-filled region, because the slicing worker receives that full array. Slicing-task payload model For a nonempty slicing task, define: Symbol Meaning V Number of spatial voxels in the box's inclusive integer extent H , W Output height and width from SliceOptions C Source channel count from CloudVolumeInterface s Source dtype item size in bytes B = sVC Bytes in the allocated source array The production download array has a channel axis, including when C = 1 . The dominant array payload during slicing is estimated as: P = B + 8V + 12HW = sVC + 8V + 12HW The 12HW term is one float32 XYZ coordinate plane reused for every assigned slice and channel. Cubic interpolation processes one channel at a time and reuses one float64 coefficient workspace, contributing 8V . Every assignment, including gapped slice indices, writes directly into temporary TIFF views. There is no accumulated heap output array or per-channel interpolation-result array. For fixed source geometry, raster, dtype, and channels, the estimate is independent of slice count and contiguity. estimate_slice_task_payload() and SliceTaskPayload own this estimate for both production partition selection and benchmark reporting. The output_bytes and channel_result_bytes components are always zero. Mapped TIFF writes/pages and the final normalization rewrite remain outside this estimate. The model describes dominant arrays for one slicing task. Process overhead, small temporary arrays, download/decode buffers, concurrently active tasks, and resident TIFF or filesystem-cache pages also affect observed memory use. A payload estimate must not be interpreted as process RSS or total run memory. The source interface is initialized before partitioning and reused by the resulting VolumeCache . Its channel count and dtype supply the cost calculation; the output dimensions come directly from SliceOptions , not from inferred rectangle edge lengths. Partition selection The reference partition uses the existing slice-count policy with the requested target_slices_per_box and max_depth . Its cumulative allocated source bytes, sum(B) , establish the work allowance. The production policy permits 0% increase over that reference. Overlapping requests count repeatedly, and zero-filled parts of requested boxes count toward the allowance. This quantity differs from source-clipped bytes, compressed storage size, and network traffic. The candidate tree is built once. At each node, proposed splits include center medians and the largest gaps between centers on each spatial axis, a gap in the assigned slice indices, and a path-order cut minimizing the larger child payload among valid cuts. Both children must be nonempty, and each child's integer volume must be at most 95% of the parent's. Child bounds always come from the full rectangle corners. The path-cut search first computes prefix and suffix corner bounds. As a cut moves forward, the prefix box can only grow and the suffix box can only shrink. Two binary searches locate the interval where both children meet the spatial rule, using BoundingBox 's inclusive volume calculation. Only cuts in that interval are scored. Every admissible cut is evaluated in its original order, preserving tie-breaking and payload-callback inputs. This avoids constructing boxes for every rejected cut without introducing a separate vectorized volume formula or assuming that task payload is monotone along the path. Candidates are compared by their largest child payload, with deterministic tie-breaking. The tree is limited by max_depth and by the availability of a valid split. Different payload thresholds select different leaves from that same tree. Selection examines thresholds at actual node payloads and the fully expanded frontier, then chooses the smallest maximum task payload within the reference work allowance. If the candidates cannot improve that maximum within the allowance, the reference partition is retained. The requested-volume allowance is checked for a complete partition. It is not charged independently at each split: an intermediate pair of boxes may contain overlap that later subdivisions remove. Planning evaluates more cuts than the count-based reference and can take longer, especially for long paths. The tree's geometry and task costs are reused across the threshold search. Reducing the estimated largest task does not guarantee faster slicing or a proportional decrease in process-tree RAM. Planning runs in VolumeCachePipelineStep . The later SliceParallelPipelineStep downloads and interpolates the selected boxes, then normalizes and writes the output. Changing the partition can therefore change that later stage's elapsed time without moving planning into it. The payload model does not optimize task execution order or completion time. With a fixed worker count, a large task dispatched late can extend the final period when other workers are idle, even if accumulated worker time decreases. Worker durations overlap and must not be added to, or equated with, the coordinator's elapsed time. Internal box ordering The slicing step normally submits downloads in partition order. Python callers can opt into alternating slice-count order when constructing the step: from ouroboros.pipeline import SliceParallelPipelineStep step = SliceParallelPipelineStep(alternate_slice_count_order=True) The keyword defaults to False and is internal to the Python pipeline; it is not a CLI, UI, or serialized SliceOptions setting. The enabled order sorts boxes by descending assigned slice count, breaking ties by original box index, then takes the first, last, next first, next last, and so on. With equal counts, the largest end takes the lower box index and the smallest end takes the higher box index. An odd middle box is submitted once. This changes download submission order. Slicing still starts as downloads complete, so concurrent tasks need not start or finish in submission order. VolumeCache remains the owner of boxes and slice assignments; the flag changes neither the partition nor the download/slicing pool sizes, in-flight limit, or box-release lifecycle. Run-statistics execution.workers records box_order as partition or alternating_slice_count for the slicing step. Alternating large and small slice counts can change task overlap, resource contention, and the final period with idle workers. It does not guarantee faster execution or lower peak memory, and slice count is not a measure of source-box volume. Keep the default unless a comparison on the intended workload supports changing it. Options, compatibility, and limits target_slices_per_box controls the count-based reference and therefore the production work allowance. It is not a maximum number of slices in a selected box. Changing it can change both the reference and the selected partition; lowering it does not guarantee lower task payload or lower observed RAM. max_depth remains the maximum subdivision depth. Raising it allows additional candidate splits but cannot overcome the spatial-reduction requirement or the size of an indivisible slice. A single oblique rectangle can require a large axis-aligned source volume. Identical rectangles and other nodes without a valid spatial reduction can also remain together with a large payload. The public calculate_bounding_boxes_bsp_link_rects helper retains its existing positional arguments and (bounding_boxes, rect_to_box_map) return shape. Geometry-only callers that omit the optional task_payload callback retain the slice-count policy. The slicing pipeline supplies that callback to enable the payload policy. The serialized BoundingBoxParams fields remain target_slices_per_box and max_depth ; their continued presence does not make the production slice-count target a hard cap. Interpolation and comparison Partition changes preserve the slice rectangles, raster dimensions, and interpolation settings. They can still change sampled values. Cubic prefiltering sees each cutout's boundaries, and float32 grid arithmetic can round differently for different integer origins. Prefilter effects decay with distance but have no universal eight-voxel, or other fixed-distance, cutoff. Their magnitude depends on the source values and local variation. A reference sampled from an individual slice's tight box has its own boundary effects. It is not automatically an exact reference for a larger box. Output comparisons should check world-coordinate agreement separately from filtering residuals and use the same source data and interpolation coordinates when isolating the filtering effect. Compare floating-point samples before final normalization as well as written outputs: normalization uses global extrema and can propagate a local sampling difference across the output. The run-statistics reference describes cumulative allocated and source-clipped download bytes and measured memory statistics. Those describe different costs and should be reported separately when evaluating a partition. Reproducing geometry comparisons Keep real specimen annotation states outside the repository. Automated tests extend the existing generated-geometry and simulated-volume fixtures; real specimen comparisons are separate benchmark observations. To regenerate recorded paths through the normal geometry pipeline without downloading specimen voxels, supply an external input directory. From python/ in the project environment, run: python benchmarks/benchmark_partitioning.py --fixtures /path/to/local-inputs --repeats 2 --output /tmp/partitioning.json The directory contains local annotation states and manifest.json . Its specimens object maps each chosen name to annotations_file (a path relative to the directory), slice_options (the existing SliceOptions geometry and bounding-box settings), source_dtype , channels , and source_scale (the source metadata's size , voxel_offset , and chunk_sizes ). Each entry also has provenance.reduced_state_sha256 for the annotation file and provenance.saved_rectangles_sha256 for the original rectangle array's bytes. These hashes detect changed inputs and report exact geometry reproduction. Annotation and output mip levels must match for offline regeneration. The report includes allocation components, slice-count distributions, index runs, repeated chunk coverage, deterministic repeated output, and planning time. Its geometry estimates are separate from the elapsed time and measured memory of a real slicing run.

docs.text: Pipeline run statistics Use --verbose with either Python CLI operation to print and save the same formatted statistics JSON: ouroboros-cli slice slice-options.json --verbose ouroboros-cli backproject backproject-options.json --verbose The report is written beside the configured outputs, using <output_file_name>-<operation>-<run_id>-statistics.json . Each invocation gets a new run identifier, so repeated runs retain their reports. This works with a single TIFF or a directory of TIFF planes. JSON numeric values retain their precision; byte counts are integers. Console headings and progress bars are outside the JSON payload. Without --verbose , the CLI skips the pipeline's accumulation of detailed timing samples, memory sampler, volume statistics, report formatting and report writes. Existing worker phase clocks still run; basic step duration and progress remain available. The pipeline factory's verbose argument continues to control its progress bar; it is separate from run reporting. Server and Docker Server tasks report statistics by default. Pass reporting_enabled=false to POST /slice/ or POST /backproject/ to disable detailed reporting for that task. Both CLI and server use the same operation lifecycle and reporting code. The existing status response and status events include statistics : { "status": "published", "path": "/configured/output/sample-slice-run-id-statistics.json", "recovery_path": null, "error": null } Publication status is pending , published , disabled , unavailable , failed , or interrupted . The API keeps a task active through required cleanup and publication; duplicate submission and deletion remain blocked while it is active. Cleanup remains part of that lifecycle when reporting is disabled. A progress read failure is exposed as progress_error without changing the scientific outcome. Docker copies scientific outputs to the host and cleans its working folder before finalizing the operation timer. It then stages and transfers the report through the existing volume server into the configured host output directory. Reports retain private file permissions ( 0600 on POSIX). For Docker exports on POSIX hosts, the volume server assigns the copied report to its host user and group so that user can read it. Windows retains Docker Desktop's host mapping. Undelivered reports are retained under /volume/main-statistics/ , outside the scientific working folder. The status response gives the recovery path. Successful delivery removes the staging copy. Normal operation and desktop shutdown cleanup preserve undelivered statistics; explicitly deleting the Docker volume also deletes those recovery copies. Scientific outcome and report-publication outcome are distinct. A failed scientific-output transfer makes the operation fail. A failed statistics write or transfer leaves a successful scientific outcome intact but exposes the publication error through status, an error event, and server logging. A console or log presentation failure is exposed separately as presentation_error ; an example is BrokenPipeError when a consumer such as head closes stdout while --verbose prints the saved report. presentation_interrupted distinguishes an interruption during this final output. Neither changes the scientific outcome or an already-published file's delivery status and path. The CLI exits with status 1 on failure and 130 on interruption, including interrupted report delivery or presentation. When options cannot be loaded and no output destination is known, the report is explicitly unavailable; no report is silently written to the current directory. Desktop status presentation The slicing and backprojection progress panels show scientific outcome and statistics publication separately. A completed task retains its final progress when report delivery fails, is interrupted, or is unavailable. The panel shows a reporting warning with the publication error and any recovery location; an unpublished path is labeled as the intended destination. Only published identifies a delivered report. Disabled reporting produces no missing-report warning. A scientific failure or interruption appears first, even when its statistics report was delivered successfully. The HTTP/SSE contract is unchanged: /status/{task_id} can return HTTP 500 with status: done , and a stream can emit error_event for successful science with a reporting problem. The desktop interprets the validated status and statistics descriptor, rather than treating the event name or aggregate error as the scientific outcome. For failed/interrupted science the aggregate error retains Task.error priority; publication and log-presentation errors are displayed separately from that descriptor. No report files are read to reconstruct status. Publication pending keeps the server status active and retains the existing submission/deletion guards. Terminal status closes its stream; events for other task IDs and events from closed/replaced streams are ignored. Connection failures or invalid status payloads close the stream and show a communication warning with the last reported progress, without declaring a scientific failure or resubmitting the task. Status messages remain in the progress panel until the stream is cleared or a new task starts, so a recovery location does not disappear with a timed alert. The existing unknown-task response ( status: error , error: Item ID Not Found , and no statistics descriptor) is also treated as an outcome-unknown warning. The stream closes and retains the last reported progress: the backend may have restarted or dropped the task, which does not establish scientific failure. This exact legacy response is recognized at the stream boundary; other scientific errors retain their normal presentation and the API contract is unchanged. The short desktop regression tests run through npm run test:release , using the Node test runner and TypeScript compiler. For individual case output, run node scripts/tests/task-status.test.mjs . They feed HTTP-shaped status bodies and simulated SSE events through the production parser, stream handler, and React progress panel; they do not exercise a full Electron GUI or perform slicing/backprojection workloads. A Docker host's OS is not inferred from the Linux container. Thread environment variables are included only when set; actual executor counts are recorded separately. docs.text: Technical Constants This page documents hardcoded implementation limits that affect Ouroboros behavior at runtime. Values here are extracted directly from the shipping source. If you change them locally, update this page in the same commit. File explorer All file explorer limits live in src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts at the top of the file, alongside the shared teardown delay in src/shared/constants.ts . They apply to the per-directory non-recursive watchers with lazy expansion that back the File Explorer panel in the Electron app. The main process keeps one non-recursive watcher per directory the user has currently expanded, plus one for the root. Expanding a subfolder starts a new watcher for it; collapsing schedules teardown after COLLAPSE_TEARDOWN_DELAY_MS , so quick collapse-then-reopen costs nothing. Watcher path-count limit Symbol: FILE_EXPLORER_WATCH_LIMIT Value: 100_000 Source: src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts line 9 Reported inside every folder-contents-error payload. Why it exists. Every watcher mirrors its discovered paths into renderer state. Even with lazy expansion, an aggressive user could open a handful of dense subfolders in sequence and still exhaust memory. One hundred thousand visible paths balances usefulness for typical scan/output folders and renderer memory use. Watcher budget. The limit is an aggregate session budget summed across every currently open watcher; a watcher's contribution is reclaimed when its folder is collapsed and torn down. Plugin enumeration budget. The same constant caps the plugin-facing get-folder-contents one-shot enumeration used by the request-directory-contents iframe message (see the plugins guide ). A plugin's recursive walk stops when the enumeration hits the cap; the response is returned with error.code: 'limit' and error.truncated: true , and nodes holds the partial result already gathered. Enumeration and watcher budgets are counted separately (the enumeration count is per-request and does not accumulate across requests), so a plugin cannot starve the file explorer by issuing many recursive requests. Once the aggregate visible add count crosses the limit, the main process emits folder-contents-error with a message of the form File explorer stopped loading after 100000 visible paths across all open folders. Collapsing a folder in the file explorer should not immediately close its watcher and drop its renderer state, because users routinely collapse-then-reopen the same folder while navigating. As soon as five hundred watcher events have accumulated in the main process, the pending queue is flushed immediately over the folder-contents-update-batch IPC channel instead of waiting for the flush interval below. The panel therefore feels responsive to individual file create/delete events while still coalescing large scans. When to reconsider. Shorten the interval if the panel feels laggy during light file activity. Lengthen it if renderer CPU during heavy scans is a problem and you would rather trade responsiveness for throughput. Plugins that need to browse the directory tree use the request-directory-contents / send-directory-contents-response message pair (see the plugins guide ) rather than depending on this broadcast payload. Main process (Electron) Plugin file server port Symbol: PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT Value: 3000 (default) Source: src/main/servers/file-server.ts line 7 Environment override: OUROBOROS_PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT (integer; unset, empty, or non-numeric values fall back to 3000 ) Why it exists. The main process forks a local Express + serve-static worker (see resources/processes/file-server-script.mjs ) that serves every installed plugin's static assets over http://127.0.0.1:3000/ by default. The renderer and plugin iframes load their index.html , icons, and any bundled JS from this server. User-visible behavior. If another process on the host is already listening on the chosen port the fork fails and plugins load with broken assets. There is no automatic fallback beyond the env override. When to reconsider. Docker volume server port Symbol: VOLUME_SERVER_PORT Value: 3001 (default) Source: src/main/servers/volume-server.ts line 7 Environment override: OUROBOROS_VOLUME_SERVER_PORT (integer; unset, empty, or non-numeric values fall back to 3001 ) Why it exists. Docker volume name Symbol: VOLUME Value: 'ouroboros-volume' Source: src/main/servers/volume-server.ts line 9, matched by the volumes.ouroboros-volume.name entry in python/compose.yml , python/compose.dev.yml , and the compose file written by scripts/prepare-production-server.mjs . The literal string 'ouroboros-volume' is duplicated across four call sites: src/main/servers/volume-server.ts , python/ouroboros/common/volume_server_interface.py , python/compose.yml , python/compose.dev.yml , and the compose file written by scripts/prepare-production-server.mjs . On app shutdown the volume server helper issues docker run --rm ... rm -rf /volume/* against this named volume. Anything else stored under the same volume name is deleted. When to reconsider. Renderer Server connection settings Symbols: DEFAULT_SERVER_URL , retryDelay Values: DEFAULT_SERVER_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:8000' retryDelay = 5000 (milliseconds) Source: src/renderer/src/contexts/ServerContext.tsx lines 4 and 41 Why it exists. User-visible behavior. The "connected" indicator can lag reality by up to about five seconds. Any fetch or stream started while the app thinks the server is down is placed on fetchQueue and replayed once the health poll flips to connected . When to reconsider. Plugin content is served locally through the plugin file server (see PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT , default port 3000), so all legitimate origins are loopback. Any port on those hosts is accepted; the port itself is env-configurable. Security note. The implementation parses event.origin with new URL(...) and compares hostname for exact equality; malformed origins fall through to a deny. Prefix matching would incorrectly accept attacker-controlled hosts such as http://localhost.evil.example . User-visible behavior. Any plugin iframe served from a non-loopback origin is silently ignored: its messages never trigger file reads, writes, or registration. When to reconsider. Python server Server host and port Symbols: HOST , PORT , DOCKER_HOST , DOCKER_PORT Values (defaults): HOST = '127.0.0.1' PORT = 8000 DOCKER_HOST = '0.0.0.0' DOCKER_PORT = 8000 Source: [ python/ouroboros/common/server.py ][py-server] lines 10-14 Environment overrides: OUROBOROS_SERVER_HOST -> HOST OUROBOROS_SERVER_PORT -> PORT (integer) OUROBOROS_DOCKER_SERVER_HOST -> DOCKER_HOST OUROBOROS_DOCKER_SERVER_PORT -> DOCKER_PORT (integer) Why it exists. Slicing/backprojection worker counts and backprojection chunk size Symbols: process_count on CommonOptions (inherited by SliceOptions and BackprojectOptions ), and chunk_size on BackprojectOptions Values: chunk_size = 160 process_count = os.cpu_count() Source: python/ouroboros/helpers/options.py User override: process_count in either operation’s options JSON; chunk_size in backprojection options. An explicit count must be at least four. Use multiples of four for an exact total worker count with the existing role splits. Omitted counts resolve to the backend logical CPU count when options are loaded. These are worker budgets, not CPU affinity or quota controls. API discovery: GET /options-schema returns JSON schemas directly from both options models, allowing clients to detect support before submitting jobs. Slicing reads its budget from SliceOptions.process_count during execution. Callers must set that options field. Slicing uses one-quarter download and three-quarters slicing workers; backprojection keeps its existing split. Why it exists. chunk_size is the per-dimension size of the processing chunk used by the backproject pipeline (see DataRange(FPShape.make_with(0), FPShape, FPShape.make_with(config.chunk_size)) in python/ouroboros/pipeline/backproject_pipeline.py ). process_count sets the parallel worker pool for the same pipeline; executor and writer processes are derived as fractions of it ( process_count // 4 * 2 or // 4 * 3 ). Why 160 specifically. The primary purpose of the chunk sizing is to enable clean backprojection - specifically clean backprojection of the flattened xyz stack. 160 is the judgment-call result for the best combination of memory and speed on standard pieces of data. Additionally, as for efficiency operations are performed on a flattened chunk, large values can cause significant slowdown and memory explsion due to change in the index bit size. On very small hosts, process_count = cpu_count() may over-subscribe and thrash; lowering it in the options JSON trades throughput for stability. When to reconsider. Tune per-run through the relevant operation’s options JSON. Edit the defaults only if a different global tuning is measured to be better across typical workloads. With the default off, repeated runs against the same source volume reuse locally cached tiles, which can hide upstream data changes but greatly speeds re-runs. When to reconsider. Without a shm_size override, Docker aggressively caps container /dev/shm at 64 MB , which the pipeline exceeds immediately. Setting it too large does not "cause" OOM: it just shifts OOM from the container-side artificial limit to actual host OOM. On high-RAM hosts you can raise the ceiling; on conservative shared hosts you can lower it to prefer the artificial limit hitting first. When to reconsider. Lower it on constrained hosts where you know the pipelines you run stay well under the limit; raise it only if you routinely see shared-memory ENOMEM errors from the server. Server image reference defaults Symbols: imageRepository , imageTag Values: imageRepository (default) = ghcr.io/chenglabresearch/ouroboros-server imageTag (default) = v${packageJson.version} (falls back to GITHUB_REF_NAME in CI) Source: scripts/prepare-production-server.mjs lines 10-14 Environment overrides: OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE_REPOSITORY , OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE_TAG , OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE_DIGEST , OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE (fully qualified reference) Why it exists. The prepare script writes an extra-resources/server/compose.yml that pulls the server image by name so packaged app installs do not need to build the container locally. User-visible behavior. With no environment overrides, packaging pulls ghcr.io/chenglabresearch/ouroboros-server:v<appVersion> . A release that has not yet published a matching image tag will fail at first startup with a docker pull error. When to reconsider. Set OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE_DIGEST to pin a specific build for a release, or point OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE at a private registry for internal builds. Preinstalled plugin pins Symbol: productionPluginPins Value: neuroglancer.tag = v1.1.1 neuroglancer.artifact = neuroglancer-plugin-v1.1.1.zip autoseg.tag = v0.4.0-beta.2 autoseg.cpuArtifact = auto-segmentation-v0.4.0-beta.2-cpu.zip autoseg.cudaArtifact = auto-segmentation-v0.4.0-beta.2-cuda.zip Source: scripts/prepare-package-flavor.mjs lines 7-16 Environment overrides: OUROBOROS_NEUROGLANCER_PLUGIN_TAG , OUROBOROS_NEUROGLANCER_PLUGIN_ARTIFACT , OUROBOROS_AUTOSEG_PLUGIN_TAG , OUROBOROS_AUTOSEG_CPU_PLUGIN_ARTIFACT , OUROBOROS_AUTOSEG_CUDA_PLUGIN_ARTIFACT Why it exists. These are the exact plugin release versions that the with-plugins-cpu and with-plugins-cuda package flavors ship. The core flavor ships no preinstalled plugins. User-visible behavior. A packaged app pins the listed plugin versions in extra-resources/preinstalled-plugins/ . First launch copies each into the user's plugin folder if the installed version is older or missing. Bump workflow. productionPluginPins and the fallback neuroglancerArtifactForTag / autosegArtifactForTag builders in scripts/prepare-package-flavor.mjs move together on every plugin release. The single-file edit lives in scripts/prepare-package-flavor.mjs : update the tags in productionPluginPins , and the fallback builders pick up the new filename shape automatically. The environment overrides above take precedence over both. When to reconsider. Update these pins whenever a new upstream plugin release becomes the intended default. Bump both the tag and the artifact filename together, since the artifact filename embeds the tag. Where the values come from Every value above was read directly from the tree at the time this page was written. The remaining file explorer constants live together as a block at the top of src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts ; the shared teardown delay lives in src/shared/constants.ts so both the main process and the renderer import the same value. If you edit any of them, update this page in the same commit so operators and plugin authors can rely on it.
